reasoningSteps: Assume n=8 distinct records and a comparison for every ordered pair (i,j) where i differs from j; self-pairs are excluded.
Fixing i leaves n-1 valid j values, so the exact count is n(n-1)=n²-n. Ignoring constant factors and lower-degree terms gives Theta(n²).
For eight records, 8×7=56 ordered comparisons. If pairs (i,j) and (j,i) are equivalent, divide by 2 to get 28 unordered comparisons.
Check the counting from the other end: 7+6+5+4+3+2+1=28, which doubles to 56 when orientation matters.
The claim “eight squared is exactly 64 valid distinct comparisons” incorrectly includes eight self-pairs; the asymptotic class is not the exact operation count.

Repeat with n=9: 72 ordered and 36 unordered. Explain how the leading quadratic term dominates n as n increases. Insert the edge C-F: the new shortest path A-C-F has two edges; removing edge D-F preserves the original three-edge route via E. reasoningSteps: Define an undirected six-vertex graph with edges (0,1),(1,2),(3,4),(4,5), and no cross-component edges.
BFS from one start covers exactly that start’s connected component, not necessarily every vertex in a disconnected graph.
A BFS from 0 visits {0,1,2} of size three; a second unvisited-start BFS from 3 visits {3,4,5}. There are two connected components.
The disjoint component sizes 3+3=6 account for every input vertex; the global visited set contains six only after both searches.
A single BFS returning three vertices does not prove the graph contains only three vertices or that the other vertices are isolated.

Add edge (2,3): the graph becomes connected and BFS from 0 reaches all six vertices, yielding one component. reasoningSteps: Define power(a,0)=1; for n>0 compute half=power(a,floor(n/2)), square it and multiply by a only when n is odd.
For exponent 13, the recursive exponent sequence is 13→6→3→1→0, so four non-base frames and one base frame occur.
Unwinding gives 3^1=3, 3^3=27, 3^6=729, and 3^13=1,594,323; the direct-product expansion has 13 factors.
Each non-base frame performs one squaring and odd n frames 13,3,1 perform three additional multiplies: 7 total multiplications here.
Counting 13 recursive levels because the exponent equals 13 is false for halving recursion; the stack depth is governed by log2(n).
For exponent 14, the sequence 14→7→3→1→0 has four non-base frames; test 3^14=4,782,969. Reference: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes/

reasoningSteps: Interpret each arrow as a permitted directed step and assume the graph is acyclic, so recursive path counting terminates.
Two paths start via A: S,A,C,T and S,A,D,T; one starts via B: S,B,C,T.
The dynamic programming recurrence ways(T)=1 and ways(v)=sum ways(successors) gives ways(C)=ways(D)=1, ways(A)=2, ways(B)=1, ways(S)=3.
Independently enumerate the three explicit paths and verify each follows directed edges without repeating a vertex.
Counting only distinct destinations or visited vertices conflates reachability with path multiplicity; node C participates in two paths.
Add B→D and a fourth path S,B,D,T becomes valid, so ways(S)=4. DAG DP reference https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes/

reasoningSteps: A tree contains a unique simple path between each pair of vertices, so diameter is the largest edge count on any pair path.
The path 6→4→2→1→3→7→8 contains six edges, and its endpoints lie at deepest opposite branches.
BFS starting from vertex 6 finds vertex 8 at distance 6, giving a candidate diameter of 6.
A second BFS from the farthest endpoint 8 attains maximum eccentricity 6; the two-BFS method is valid on trees.
Counting seven vertices in the path as seven edges introduces an off-by-one error; diameter is defined here in edges.

Delete leaf 8 and its incident edge; the diameter decreases to five edges on path 6→4→2→1→3→7. Tree search context https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes/
